Table of Contents

There are two common ways to use margin in a trading account: cross margin and isolated margin. Cross margin involves margin that is shared between open positions. Isolated margin, on the other hand, is margin assigned to a single position that is restricted from being shared.

Cross margin may help prevent quick liquidations and has a better capability to withstand portfolio losses. Isolated margin offers better flexibility in that other portfolio holdings will not be affected if a single position is liquidated.

Key Points

• Cross margin is a system that allows traders to share margin across positions and accounts by using excess margin from one account to collateralize positions in a different account.

• Cross margining can help prevent a single losing position from causing a margin call or forced liquidation.

• Isolated margin is using only a single position as leverage for borrowing.

• Isolated margin can protect larger portfolio holdings from margin calls or forced liquidation because it limits leverage to only a single position.

• Cross margining can be an effective risk-management tool, particularly for long-term positions, because it increases available liquidity, which protects the investment during periods of volatility.

## What Is Cross Margin?

Cross margin was introduced in the late 1980s as a way to reduce systematic risk in the market and to help traders better manage their portfolios when engaging in [margin trading](https://www.sofi.com/learn/investing/what-is-margin-trading/).

At the institutional level, cross margin offsets the value of hedged positions maintained by firms at multiple clearinghouses. Cross margining recognizes intermarket hedged positions, thus allowing for reduced [initial margin requirements](https://www.sofi.com/learn/content/what-is-initial-margin/), fewer margin variations, and smaller net settlements.

For individual traders, cross margin provides more leeway in how open positions in a portfolio move. Cross margin takes excess margin from one margin account and gives it to another to satisfy [maintenance margin requirements](https://www.sofi.com/learn/content/what-is-maintenance-margin/). That sharing of margin allows the trader to use all available margin balances across their accounts.

### How Does Cross Margin Work?

Cross margin is not a simple calculation, and it runs on sophisticated algorithms. By sharing margin across accounts, traders can access more exposure without depositing more capital. Clearinghouses, [central counterparties](https://www.sofi.com/learn/content/central-counterparty/), and brokers determine cross margin amounts and automatically move margin between accounts that have registered for the service.

Traders might prefer cross margining, as a single losing position might not be liquidated quickly when market conditions change. Excess margin is transferred from another account to meet a minor shortfall in minimum maintenance. Cross margin helps to avoid quick [margin calls](https://www.sofi.com/learn/content/what-is-a-margin-call/) and forced liquidations.

Be sure to understand the terms of the margin account, though, as buying on margin includes the risk of bigger losses.

### How to Use Cross Margin

Cross margin is best used when a trader has multiple margin trading accounts. A [cash account and margin account work differently](https://www.sofi.com/learn/content/cash-account-vs-margin-account/), and cross vs. isolated margin only applies to the latter type. For traders concerned about a single position being stopped out, it is generally better for them to use cross margin vs. isolated margin, as the former is a tool to help prevent unnecessary forced liquidations. So, a trader must trade with a broker who offers this service.

Volatile markets demonstrate the benefits of cross vs. isolated margin. With cross margin, when there are extreme movements in single securities, it is hard to keep a handle on individual positions’ margin requirements. Cross margining can calculate amounts automatically and move excess margin to other accounts that need it.

## What Is Isolated Margin?

Isolated margin is margin assigned to a single position that is restricted to a specific amount. When the allocated margin drops below an unrealized profit and loss threshold or the maintenance margin requirement, the trader may face a margin call or potentially a liquidation of their assets.

The upshot is that other positions in the account are not affected. Isolated vs. cross margin tends to offer better flexibility because it can divide the trader’s funds, but stop-outs can happen quickly in volatile markets. Isolated margin vs. cross margin are different from each other, and both are used in crypto trading. It’s important to know [what decentralized exchanges are](https://www.sofi.com/crypto-basics/) when using either margin type when buying and selling crypto.

### How Does Isolated Margin Work?

Isolated margin works by setting aside a margin amount for a single position. Volatile and [speculative positions](https://www.sofi.com/learn/content/speculative-investment/) are sometimes good candidates for the use of isolated margin. It can be helpful when you don’t want other portfolio holdings to be impacted by a change in the value or margin requirements from that single position.

# Cross Margin vs. Isolated Margin: Understanding the Differences in Crypto Trading

A single decision in the crypto markets can catapult your portfolio to new heights — or lead to a fast depletion of funds. For example: Do you know if you should opt for cross margin, risking your entire account balance on market shifts, or isolated margin, limiting risk to a specific trade? This decision can define the thin line between a strategic win and an unforeseen setback. Choosing the right margin strategy isn’t just a matter of preference, but a critical component of risk management.We’ll outline the differences between cross margin vs isolated margin in the context of leverage trading in cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin (BTC) and Ethereum (ETH). Whether you're a seasoned investor or a [beginner](https://alphapoint.com/blog/best-crypto-for-beginners) in the crypto trading scene, understanding these concepts is key to navigating such a volatile market.

## Understanding Margin Trading

[Margin trading](https://alphapoint.com/trading/derivatives-margin-markets) means you're not just using your funds, but you're also leveraging borrowed money to increase your buying power. Here's a brief look at how this works:

- **Initial margin:** This is your starting capital, the collateral you deposit to open a position.
- **Leverage:** Expressed as a ratio (such as 2:1), leverage multiplies your potential trade value based on your initial margin requirements.
- **Maintenance margin:** This is the minimum amount of equity you need to maintain in your margin account to keep a position open.

If you place $10,000 in a margin account and use 2X leverage, you can initiate a trade worth $20,000. Your capacity for both profit and loss is amplified. While regular trading confines your potential to the amount you've invested, margin trading enables a heightened capacity for return — but with that comes an increased risk.

### Margin Trading vs. Regular Trading

Margin trading and regular trading are distinct approaches in the financial markets, primarily differentiated by leverage use. In regular trading, investors use their own capital to buy digital assets, limiting potential returns to the amount invested. On the other hand, margin trading allows traders to borrow funds from a broker, amplifying their buying power. This leverage can significantly increase potential returns — a small market movement can lead to substantial gains. However, it also escalates risk. The same market fluctuation can result in equally magnified losses. Margin trading requires a smaller initial capital outlay but involves the risk of losing more than the initial investment, unlike regular trading, where the risk is typically limited to the invested capital.

## What Is Cross Margin?

Cross margin is a strategy where your entire margin account serves as the collateral for all your open positions. When you engage in cross margin trading, you're distributing the risk across all your assets, which can help guard against liquidation risk.As a capital efficiency measure, cross margin lets you use multiple assets within your trading account as collateral. So, you won't need to close leveraged positions to free up funds. Removing the chore of earmarking specific margin amounts to individual positions streamlines trade management.Of course, cross margin isn't without its drawbacks. When you use it, you expose your entire account balance to the market's volatility. If the market takes a downturn, you face a higher risk of total account liquidation. This strategy can also reduce your precision in managing risk for each trade since your entire account's worth fluctuates with market movements.

### Pros and Cons of Cross Margin Trading

**Pros of cross margin:**

- Risk distribution across assets
- Prevents single asset liquidation from immediate impact
- Enhances capital efficiency
- Simplifies trade management

**Cons of cross margin:**

- Greater risk of total account liquidation
- Lower control of individual position risks
- Full account balance affected by market shifts

Cross margin could be a fitting choice if you’re seeking to maximize your trading power and are comfortable with the higher stakes it brings. Make sure to consider both your investment strategy and risk tolerance before opting for cross margin trading.

## What Is Isolated Margin?

Isolated Margin is another risk management strategy used in cryptocurrency trading. When you opt for isolated margin, you decide to allocate a set amount of your capital exclusively to a single trading position. This practice is distinct because the funds you've assigned are strictly ring-fenced from your overall account balance.Why use isolated margin? It gives you precise control over the potential risk associated with your position. You're saying, “This is the maximum I'm willing to lose on this trade.” Should the market move against you, liquidation happens only for the specified amount, safeguarding the rest of your funds.In isolated margin, leverage works within the boundaries of your specific position. It's a double-edged sword, though: While it can amplify your gains, it can also heighten losses, triggering a margin call if the market moves unfavorably and your position nears liquidation.

### Pros and Cons of Isolated Margin Trading

**Pros of isolated margin:**

- Granularity: Offers more nuanced risk controls.
- Risk limitation: Limits potential losses to only the margin allotted to the position.

**Cons of isolated margin:**

- Lower capital efficiency: Isolating funds can tie up capital that might be used in other trades.
- Vigilance required: Constant monitoring of market shifts and possible additional collateral deposits.
- Flexibility: May be less compared to cross margin since funds can't automatically shift to support other positions

## What Is Isolated Margin Trading?

**Isolated margin trading**assigns a fixed amount of margin to each position. Isolated margin offers traders the ability to allocate collateral individually to each particular position, providing precise risk management and risk control. If that trade goes against you, only the collateral assigned to that particular position is at risk, protecting other positions.

**Benefits of isolated margin**:

- Limits your losses to the margin allocated for that trade
- Offers better control over individual position risks, allowing you to carefully manage position sizes and ensuring that only the collateral assigned to a particular position is at risk, which protects other positions in your portfolio
- Easy to manage for beginner or part-time traders

**Downsides**:

- If margin is too small, you can get liquidated fast
- Doesn’t allow gains in one trade to buffer losses in another
- Requires more active monitoring

## Cross Margin vs Isolated Margin

**Key differences**between cross margin and isolated margin include how margin requirements, collateral allocations, and margin assigned to each trading position are handled. In cross margin, the margin and collateral are shared across your entire portfolio, meaning losses in one position can impact your whole trading account. In contrast, isolated margin assigns a specific margin to each trading position, limiting risk to that position and protecting the rest of your entire portfolio. The choice of margin type directly affects your risk exposure, margin requirements, and how you manage your trading account.

Derivatives trading is one of the most popular ways for crypto traders to make money. Trading in derivatives and [CFDs (contracts for difference)](https://themoneymongers.com/exchanges/crypto-cfd-brokers/) allows traders to amplify their gains by opening leveraged positions.

If you are just getting into this segment of cryptocurrency trading, you will come across the terms cross and isolated margin. The two are the main modes of margin management in many exchanges, and [many leading crypto exchanges](https://themoneymongers.com/exchanges/how-many-crypto-exchanges-are-there/) make them interchangeable.

Traders need to know what the two margin management modes are all about, as this makes it easy to decide what to use when opening their positions. This guide looks at what the two margin modes in more detail.

## What Is Cross margin In Cryptos?

Cross margin means that the margin will be shared across all open positions. With cross margin, all the funds in your available balance can be utilized regardless of your initial margin when opening the position.

Cross or [spread](https://themoneymongers.com/exchanges/what-is-spread-in-crypto/) margin, as many traders will also refer to it will utilize any funds in your available balance to [avoid liquidation](https://themoneymongers.com/exchanges/what-is-liquidation-in-crypto-trading/). 

The cross margin mode is handy for [crypto traders hedging on their existing positions](https://themoneymongers.com/exchanges/crypto-futures-for-hedging/) and for arbitragers that want to prevent exposure on one side of their trade-in case of liquidation. Cross margin helps minimize liquidation risk as the crypto traders use their account balance as a source of extra margin.

While cross margin has many benefits, it will also give the traders less control when managing the available funds in their accounts.

That said, traders need to note that any unrealized profits from your open positions will not be part of the available funds in your account. Therefore, these funds cannot be utilized for cross margin. However, any profits already realized from other positions can be utilized in cross margin for other positions using the same settlement crypto.

Note: The cross margin mode will be default for all positions in most [crypto leverage trading platforms](https://themoneymongers.com/exchanges/crypto-margin-trading-platforms/). Therefore, you should remember to change it to open an isolated margin position.

### What Is Isolated margin In Cryptos?

When a crypto trader opens an isolated margin trade, the initial margin required to open the position will be kept separate from the account’s available balance. The margin is also separate from what you use to open other positions.

What all this means is that with an isolated margin, your position will be liquidated as soon as your margin goes below the required maintenance margin. With an isolated margin, other funds in your available balance cannot be used to restore the margin to the maintenance level to prevent liquidation.

An isolated margin offers more security and gives traders peace of mind when opening speculative positions that are riskier. The traders will never lose more than their initial margin with an isolated margin. This margin mode never taps into your available balance account regardless of the situation.

Another advantage of isolated margin is that the traders get more control over individual positions, unlike when using cross margin.

Like cross margin, the initial margin also has its shortcomings. Among these shortcomings is that using it when opening positions with high leverage puts you at a more significant liquidation risk. For example, if you use an isolated margin to open a position with 100x leverage, just a 1% fall in price is enough to trigger liquidation.

### **How Does Cross Margin/Leverage Work?**

Cross margin or leverage will utilize the total amount of funds in the trader’s available balance account to prevent liquidation if your position goes below the maintenance margin.

The cross margin will be calculated using the maximum leverage allowed for the trading pair when using the cross margin mode. However, all the positions need to have similar settlement crypto for cross margin to work.

An example should make it easier to understand cross margin. Suppose you have 2 BTC in your account and want to open a cross margin position with 0.01 BTC using a platform with [100x maximum leverage](https://themoneymongers.com/exchanges/what-does-100x-leverage-mean-in-crypto/). 

In this case, the value of your full position is 1 BTC (0.01 x 100) when using maximum leverage. You will need an initial margin requirement of 0.01 BTC if the company requires 1% to open the position.

If there is a decrease in [BTC Futures](https://themoneymongers.com/exchanges/what-are-bitcoin-futures/) price by a small percentage, the trader’s position will not be liquidated. Instead, the cross margin mode will utilize the 1.99 BTC remaining in your account to increase the margin. 

Cross margin will keep utilizing the funds in your account to increase your margin if the price keeps dropping. Hence, you can lose both the amount you use to open the position and what is in your available balance with cross margin.

### **How Does Isolated Margin Work?**

With an isolated margin, you can only increase your margin by adding more funds to your position as you cannot utilize what is in your available balance. While this means you can only lose what you use to open the position, it also means your position can get to liquidation level quickly.

Suppose you have 2 BTC and want to open an isolated margin position with 0.01 BTC using 100x leverage in a platform that supports it. In this case, the size of your full position will be 1 BTC (100 x 0.01).
